item.title: The Code of Ethics and the Standards of Professional Conduct: the Map
item.summary: Every CFA candidate must follow one short Code of Ethics made of six principles and a set of Standards of Professional Conduct grouped under seven headings. This lesson gives you the layout so you can name each piece and place a scenario under the right heading.

sections.heading: Why there are two layers
sections.body_markdown:
Think of a country's constitution and its detailed laws. The **Code of Ethics** is the short statement of principles, and the **Standards of Professional Conduct** are the more specific conduct rules that put those principles into practice.

Both apply to CFA Institute members (including charterholders) and to candidates in the CFA Program, wherever they work and whatever their job. Firms are encouraged to adopt them too, but the Code and Standards are written for individuals.

sections.heading: The six components of the Code of Ethics
sections.body_markdown:
Each component is a promise about how you behave. In my own words:

1. **Act ethically and respectfully**, with integrity, competence and diligence, toward everyone you deal with: the public, clients, prospects, employers, colleagues and other market participants.
2. **Put others first.** The integrity of the profession and your clients' interests come before your own personal interests.
3. **Use reasonable care and independent professional judgment** in analysis, recommendations, actions and other professional activities.
4. **Practice professionally and encourage others to do the same**, in a way that reflects well on you and on the profession.
5. **Promote the integrity and viability of global capital markets**, for the benefit of society.
6. **Maintain and improve your own competence**, and try to help other investment professionals improve theirs.

Memory aid: each one starts with a verb, *Act, Place, Use, Practice, Promote, Maintain*.

sections.heading: The seven Standards of Professional Conduct
sections.body_markdown:
The Standards are grouped under seven numbered headings. For this objective you only need the headings and their order:

- **I. Professionalism**
- **II. Integrity of Capital Markets**
- **III. Duties to Clients**
- **IV. Duties to Employers**
- **V. Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions**
- **VI. Conflicts of Interest**
- **VII. Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate**

A helpful way to see them is by *who or what you owe duties to*. Standard I is about you and your own conduct, II is the markets, III is clients, IV is your employer, V is the quality of your analysis and communication, VI is conflicts, and VII is your standing in the CFA Institute community.

The lettered parts under each Standard, such as I(A) or III(C), belong to a different learning objective and are not needed here.

sections.heading: Using the map on exam day
sections.body_markdown:
Exam questions often describe a situation and ask which Standard is involved. First decide whose interests are affected: the market, a client, the employer, or the CFA community. That usually narrows the answer to one heading.

Note the numbering. Standards are labelled with Roman numerals, and the Code of Ethics has no numbers at all, only six bullet-style principles. The Standards also reflect the Code: for example, the Code asks you to maintain competence, and the Standards have a Competence provision inside Standard I (this was added to the Standards in the 2024 handbook edition).

worked_example.problem: A research analyst at an investment firm does three things in one week. (a) She hears a rumour that a takeover bid is about to be announced and buys the shares for her own account before it is public. (b) She quietly does paid consulting work for another firm without telling her employer. (c) She recommends a stock to a client without any analysis to back it up. Match each action to the heading of the Standards of Professional Conduct that is most directly concerned.
steps: Action (a): trading on information that the public does not yet have harms fairness in the market. The affected party is the market, so this falls under Standard II, Integrity of Capital Markets.
Action (b): hiding outside paid work affects her employer. The affected party is the employer, so this falls under Standard IV, Duties to Employers.

Action (c): a recommendation with no supporting analysis concerns the quality of her investment analysis and recommendations. This falls under Standard V, Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions.
No calculation is needed, so no calculator keystrokes are required.
worked_example.answer: (a) Standard II; (b) Standard IV; (c) Standard V.

exam_traps: Mixing up the counts: the Code of Ethics has six components and the Standards have seven headings.
Treating the Code and Standards as applying only to charterholders. Candidates in the CFA Program are covered as well.
Confusing Standard IV (Duties to Employers) with Standard III (Duties to Clients), or Standard II (markets) with Standard III. Ask whose interests are at stake.
Forgetting Standard VII. It is about your responsibilities as a member or candidate in CFA Institute programs, and it is the one most often left off a recalled list.
Mixing up the order of the Roman numerals, for example placing Conflicts of Interest at V instead of VI.

item.stem: Which of the following is one of the six components of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics?

options.text: Give priority to the employer's interests over client interests
options.explanation: This reverses the Code. Clients' interests and the integrity of the profession come before personal interests, and employer loyalty never overrides duties to clients.

options.text: Maintain and improve professional competence and help others do likewise
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping your own competence up, and striving to raise that of other investment professionals, is one of the six Code principles.

options.text: Follow the more lenient of any conflicting laws or regulations
options.explanation: This reverses the rule found in the Standards: when laws conflict, you follow the stricter one. It is also not one of the six Code components.

item.stem: Which of the following is the title of one of the seven Standards of Professional Conduct?

options.explanation: Correct. Standard IV is titled Duties to Employers.
There is no Standard with this name. Obligations toward regulators are handled inside other Standards, such as the one on knowledge of the law.
No such Standard exists. The Standards apply to members and candidates, not to companies that issue securities.

item.stem: Which pairing of Standard number and title is correct?

options.explanation: Mixed-up numbering. Standard II is Integrity of Capital Markets; Duties to Clients is Standard III.
Mixed-up numbering. Standard V is Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions; Conflicts of Interest is Standard VI.
Correct. Duties to Employers is Standard IV, sitting between Duties to Clients (III) and Investment Analysis (V).

item.stem: A portfolio manager buys shares for her own account after learning, through a friend at a law firm, of a merger that has not been announced. Which heading of the Standards of Professional Conduct is most directly concerned?

options.explanation: No client relationship is the focus here. Candidates pick this because she is a portfolio manager, but the harm is to fairness in the market.

options.text: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets
options.explanation: Correct. Trading on material information that is not public undermines market integrity, which is the subject of Standard II.
Her employer is not the central issue. Candidates choose this because of the personal trade, but the core concern is the markets.

item.stem: An analyst takes on paid weekend work for a competitor of her employer and does not tell her employer. Which heading of the Standards of Professional Conduct is most directly concerned?

options.explanation: Correct. Keeping an employer unaware of outside paid work relates to the obligations owed to the employer under Standard IV.
This is a tempting choice because a competitor is involved, but the main concern is the duty owed to the employer, not a conflict affecting clients or analysis.

options.text: Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
options.explanation: No analysis or recommendation is involved in the facts, so this heading is not the best fit.

item.stem: Which statement best describes how the Code of Ethics and the Standards of Professional Conduct relate to each other?

options.text: The Code has seven principles and the Standards have six headings
options.explanation: The counts are swapped. The Code has six components and the Standards have seven headings.

options.text: They apply only to charterholders, not to candidates in the CFA Program
options.explanation: Wrong scope. They apply to CFA Institute members, including charterholders, and to candidates.

options.text: The Code sets out broad principles and the Standards turn them into conduct rules
options.explanation: Correct. The six-part Code gives the principles and the seven groups of Standards apply them to professional conduct.

item.stem: A CFA Program candidate shares questions from the Level I exam with a friend who is registered for the next sitting. Which heading of the Standards of Professional Conduct most directly covers this conduct?

options.text: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets
options.explanation: The conduct has nothing to do with trading or market information. Exam content is not market information about securities.

options.text: Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate
options.explanation: Correct. Standard VII covers how members and candidates behave as participants in CFA Institute programs, including exam conduct.
No client is involved. Candidates sometimes choose this because it is the best-known duty heading, but it does not fit the facts.

item.front: How many components does the CFA Institute Code of Ethics have, and what verbs start them?
item.back: Six: Act (ethically), Place (others' interests above your own), Use (reasonable care and independent judgment), Practice (and encourage others to), Promote (market integrity), Maintain (and improve competence).

item.front: List the seven Standards of Professional Conduct in order.
item.back: I Professionalism; II Integrity of Capital Markets; III Duties to Clients; IV Duties to Employers; V Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions; VI Conflicts of Interest; VII Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate.
